title: Busy Leaders Insist a Complaint Must Be Followed by a Solution
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Argues that empowered, trusted teams generate more complaints, not because people are unhappier but because they feel safer voicing dissatisfaction -- and that good leaders manage the volume by requiring a proposed solution alongside every complaint. Walks through the mechanics: when a team member can't offer a remedy, the leader sends them back to think it through rather than dismissing the complaint outright. The piece frames this as shifting mindset from problem-focused to solution-focused, turning venting into ownership. Notes that some complaints simply evaporate once a solution is required, which the piece treats as a feature, not a suppression of legitimate concerns.
points: Requiring a proposed solution alongside every complaint filters venting from genuine, actionable concerns without shutting down the complaint channel.
The practice shifts team members from 'observer to contributor and from victim to advocate' by making them own the fix, not just name the problem.
Complaints that disappear once a solution is required are usually more emotional than substantive -- an intended outcome, as long as legitimate issues still surface.
quotes: When team members feel empowered, trusted, and safe, they speak up more freely. It’s not that members of empowered teams are unhappier; it’s just that they feel more comfortable voicing their views.

To make sure team members feel strongly about what they advocate for and to reduce the number of unnecessary complaints they hear, good leaders insist on a simple rule: They require team members to offer a solution after raising any complaint.
Leaders who follow this rule not only receive fewer complaints that waste their time but also help team members to shift their mindset from problem-focused to solution-focused.
By asking team members to replace their venting with a “diagnosis and propose” mentality, leaders move people from observer to contributor and from victim to advocate.

Of course, some complaints disappear when a team member must think through a solution, usually because the issue is more emotional than substantive. This is the ideal outcome as long as the practice doesn’t silence legitimate concerns.
Good leaders insist that team members “own the fix” of any problem they raise by showing them how. With modest repetition, this cuts down on repetitive venting that wastes everyone’s time.
